utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: The witness was present in Bratunac throughout the events surrounding the fall of the Srebrenica enclave. On 9 July, 1995 at around noon, the witness visited the 3rd Battalion logistics base located in Pribicevac accompanied by the Bratunac Brigade's assistant commander for logistics, Dragoslav Trisic. There the witness encountered the assistant commander for religious, moral, and legal affairs of the VRS Main Staff, General Milan Gvero. General Radislav Krstic, then the Chief of Staff of the Drina Corps, was also present that afternoon and discussed the operation of -- discussed the operation of the separate -- operation to separate the Srebrenica and Zepa enclaves with General Gvero. Also present was whom the witness referred to as Colonel Vukota, presumably Colonel Vukota Vukovic, commander of the Skelani Brigade. On 11 July, 1995, the witness returned to the 3rd Battalion logistics base. On this occasion he briefly encountered General Ratko Mladic, later near the base's command post, he met among others, Miroslav Deronjic, president of the Municipal Board of the SDS, and Miodrag Josipovic, the Bratunac chief of police. That evening, the witness received a call from Deronjic who told him to attend a meeting at the Bratunac Brigade command at 8.00 am on the following morning, 12th July. That morning the witness went to the Bratunac Brigade command, he was the first to arrive and recalled that General Mladic asked him what he thought should be done with the Muslims in Srebrenica. The witness testified that knowing that in 1992, the Muslims had gone to Tuzla and Kladanj, he said to General Mladic, "We should see what these people wanted at the moment." Mladic put the same question to Aco Tesic, head of the secretariat for national Defence, who later arrived, as well as to Ljubisav Simic, president of Bratunac municipality, when he arrived. The meeting lasted approximately 30 minutes and upon its conclusion, General Mladic asked the witness and Simic to attend the meeting at the Hotel Fontana at 10.00 a.m. The witness recalled that present at the meeting were General Mladic, General Krstic, the UNPROFOR commander and his deputy, Ibro Nuhanovic, whom the witness knew well, Nesib Mandzic, Camila Purkovic, Ljubisav Simic, Dragomir Vasic, and Miroslav Deronjic. He testified that it was his understanding that the Muslim population had decided to leave the region. Following the meeting, General Mladic asked the witness and Simic were providing for the population gathered in Potocari. The witness returned to his offices to co-ordinate the effort. He testified that he secured two water cisterns, contacted a bakery to send its produce to Potocari, and tried to secure other supplies from Zvornik. Efforts were made -- also made to obtain supplies from Serbian municipalities, including Ljubovija. On 12 July, the witness was present in Potocari for about two hours, during which he stated he helped to distribute bread, biscuits, and water. Among the refugees, the witness recognised several people whom he knew. He was able to assist two or three of them. The witness claimed that he did not see any Muslim men being separated from their family, but noted that the population "all wanted to get on the buses out of turn just so they he could leave Potocari as soon as possible." The witness left Potocari and returned to Bratunac, returning to his office later that afternoon. At around 8.00 p.m. the director of the utilities enterprise, Dragan Mirkovic, visited the witness. Later at about 9.00 p.m. the witness noticed three buses parked near the town's municipal building guarded by civilian police. Together with Mirkovic the witness went to observe the situation more closely and eventually noticed three other buses nearby. Each was filled with Muslim men. The witness recognised some of the prisoners aboard the bus, one of whom asked him for water. The witness complied passing out jerrycans of water to prisoners aboard two buses. The witness eventually learned that some 20 to 25 buses had come to Bratunac and was told that the Muslim men were to be exchanged. That night, the witness ran into Miroslav Deronjic in town. Discussing the unfolding situation with him, Deronjic told the witness that the situation had been influenced by Rajko Dukic, a powerful politico and director of the bauxite mine in Milici. The witness testified that in addition to the local police guarding bus throughout the town, other security measures were taken. Because most fighting-aged men in Bratunac were manning the lines, older town residents and younger people were quickly rounded up to assist in guarding the prisoners. At a concern point, either that evening or the following morning, the witness learned that Muslim men had also been detained at the Vuk Karadzic school in Bratunac. On 13 July, the witness went to see Dragoslav Trisic, who told the witness that Resid Sinanovic, the former chief of police in Bratunac, had been captured. The witness learned that Sinanovic was in the custody of Zlatan Celanovic, who was a Legal Officer in the Bratunac Brigade and conducted investigations. The witness contacted Celanovic and arranged to see Sinanovic. He later met with Sinanovic in Celanovic's office for about an hour. The witness learned that Sinanovic was to be taken to the Vuk Karadzic school. At about 7.00 a.m. on 14 July, the witness learned about mass killings at the Kravica warehouse which occurred in the afternoon of 13 July, he learned this from Jovan Nikolic and Dragan Nikolic, both directors of the co-operative in Kravica. Later that morning at about 9.30 a.m. the witness was called to the SDS party offices. When he arrived he met a VRS officer in uniform who introduced himself as Beara. After exchange of pleasantries, Beara invited the witness to a neighbouring office to talk to two other VRS officers. The witness recalled only that these officers were a lieutenant-colonel and colonel respectively. The two officers questioned the witness about the obtaining construction equipment, and the witness told them about a SKIP, which is a digging machine located a utilities company, and an ULT, U-L-T, which is a loader located at a Brickworks factory. The witness further contacted the director of the of the Brickworks factory Nedzo Nikolic. Although the officers did not tell the witness what they sought the equipment for, the witness assumed in the circumstance that the equipment was needed to bury people.

utterances.text: Could you please repeat the number, you left out one part of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I am sure I did I am sorry. It's 0291-6185.

utterances.speaker: PW-063

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I think for the record we have an indication that you said the name Nesib Nuhanovic, previously you mentioned Nesib Mandzic. Is that who you've referred to again?

utterances.speaker: PW-063

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Proceeding with this photograph, can you tell us who the officer is to the far right of the photograph?

utterances.speaker: PW-063
utterances.text: General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And can you tell us from this photograph, you can only see really the back of the hair or the back of the head, I should say, of this person, who that person is seated next to General Mladic on his left?

utterances.speaker: PW-063
utterances.text: I think that that is Petar, the interpreter.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. I'd like to show you another photograph. This should correspond to page 40 of the -- in e-court of P624. And its ERN is 0291-6187. Do you recognise anybody depicted in this photograph, witness?

utterances.speaker: PW-063
utterances.text: The first on the right is Dragomir Masic the chief of the public security centre in Zvornik, he is wearing a camouflage uniform. Next to him is Miroslav Deronjic, in a white shirt, and a black jacket. Next to Miroslav Deronjic is Colonel Popovic, I believe. He is drinking, he is drinking water from a glass. And then the two officers on the right side of Colonel Popovic, I don't know them. They are wearing uniforms, that's why I'm saying they are officers. I assume they are, but I don't know their names.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: The last name of the first person you identified isn't clear in the transcript, can you please repeat the last name of the first individual you?

utterances.speaker: PW-063
utterances.text: Vasic. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And you mentioned Colonel Popovic. Did you know Colonel Popovic at the time?

utterances.speaker: PW-063
utterances.text: No, I didn't. But I believe that I recognise his face.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. And -- all right. I think we are clear. Thank you very much. I think we are done with these photographs and there are just a couple of questions I'd like to ask you. Earlier just a few moments ago while I was reading a summary, I mentioned the name Rajko Dukic. His name was mentioned in a conversation with Miroslav Deronjic on 12 July, 1995. Can you tell us, first, who Rajko Dukic was at the time.

utterances.speaker: PW-063
utterances.text: Rajko Dukic was a man who hailed from Milici. That's where he was born. He was the director of the bauxite mine in Milici.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And as concerns a conversation with Miroslav Deronjic concerning Rajko Dukic, can you tell us generally what that conversation was about?

utterances.speaker: PW-063
utterances.text: On the 12th in the evening, I saw Miroslav Deronjic in town on the street. I asked him, "What is this, Deronjic? How come these buses with Muslims are in Bratunac?" And Miroslav answered, and I will quote him, "Rajko Dukic has arranged that. He has planted that upon us."

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: What did you understand Mr. Deronjic to mean by that?

utterances.speaker: PW-063
utterances.text: What he meant was that Rajko had done that in order to avoid crowds and such large presence of Muslims in Milici. He used his authority to turn the buses and the whole transport towards Bratunac. That's what Deronjic meant. And based on what he said and how he saw the situation, I also realised that that must have been the reason why the buses had arrived in Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And was Rajko Dukic at the time a politically influential person?

utterances.speaker: PW-063
utterances.text: Yes. He was the highest authority in the Birac region. In 1992 he was the president of the Serbian Democratic Party, I think, in Bosnia and later on in Republika Srpska. And he was also as I've already stated the highest authority in the Birac region. He was a well known businessman and he had a lot of influence, a very big say in the region.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you about your meeting with Colonel Beara on the 14th of July, 1995 in the morning. First, can you tell us how long you met with him?

utterances.speaker: PW-063
utterances.text: My meeting with Colonel Beara was only about 10 minutes long. That's how long I stayed in the office where we met.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Had you seen him in Bratunac prior to that meeting?

utterances.speaker: PW-063

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And having heard about him prior to meeting him, what did you know about him?

utterances.speaker: PW-063

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I thank you very much, witness, I have no further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Vanderpuye. Mr. Tolimir, your cross-examination, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I would like to say good afternoon to the witness, and may these proceedings end in keeping with God's will and not necessarily the way I want them to finish. I'm first going to ask you based on what Mr. Vanderpuye asked you and what you stated in your statement --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, are you referring to the Popovic transcript? You didn't mention that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This is P866 and P867 respectively. Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. We are in open session. Can we go into private session for a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think it's more helpful for everybody that we move into private session and then the witness can provide you with details. We go into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are back in open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Witness, I am restricted in the scope of questions I can put to you with regard to your position and duties. Why don't you tell the Trial Chamber yourself whether you encountered any problems with regard to the supply of food and providing food to the population procurement in the -- in your capacity as you performed your duties?

utterances.speaker: PW-063
utterances.text: Of course we had problems, but our problems were of financial nature. There was no money, there was not enough money and you needed money for everything. Very few companies worked. We felt an acute shortage of money and that was our major logistical problem. I don't know whether you had that in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I had in mind. Did you have any problem with the shortage of fuel or electricity and other resources pertaining to that sector?

utterances.speaker: PW-063
utterances.text: To a great fortune we did not have any problems with electricity, owing to the fact that we are close to Serbia. We got our electricity supplies from Serbia. That meant that Bratunac had electric energy throughout the war without any interruptions. We had problems with fuel, with oil, and oil derivatives, petrol. We had some problems with utilities, with water, for example, only for a couple of months when the well had fallen into the Muslim hands and that's where Bratunac gets its water-supply and that was only for two months and that's when we are talking about water.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. How did you get water at the time? Did you request from the Muslims to allow you to get your water-supply?

utterances.speaker: PW-063
utterances.text: We had an old waterworks in town that had not functioned for awhile so we brought it into function but that wasn't enough. People used water-pumps and they also got water from streams, brooks, and from the Drina River depending on how far they lived from the water. We never asked the Muslims anything nor did they ever allow us to use the new waterworks, the new well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please tell us whether you were familiar with the situation in the enclave of Srebrenica from 1993 when Srebrenica had become a demilitarised zone until the year 1995 while the population was still there, and I particularly mean the humanitarian situation?

utterances.speaker: PW-063
utterances.text: Yes, I knew the situation partially. I knew that the humanitarian situation over there was quite critical. The UNHCR convoys that supplied Srebrenica with certain necessities such as food and other such things did pass through Bratunac, but I know that the situation was quite difficult over there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell us what the military situation was like in that enclave after the demilitarisation? Do you have any information about that? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-063
utterances.text: Well, the military situation hadn't changed a great deal after a demilitarisation. The Muslims continued to attack our lines, our villages, so what happened very often were incursions in these villages with very tragic consequences. Practically the demilitarisation wasn't felt at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell the Trial Chamber of a particular case that you are aware of because that was the territory of your municipality in respect of these tragic situations that you had just referred to at the time? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-063
utterances.text: Well, we had this tragic situation in Bjelovac when during one day 109 persons were killed. Out of them, 90 per cent were civilians. In the month of January on Christmas day in Kravica, 60 persons were killed. There was another situation in Bjelovac when 30-something people were killed, then in Pakovici [as interpreted] 25, in the territory of Srebrenica those were the most serious mass killings that took place.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I do apologise because I will have to go back to this for the transcript. Can you tell us when these 109 persons were killed in Bjelovac, 90 per cent of who were civilians? In which period this happened?

utterances.speaker: PW-063
utterances.text: I think it was December 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. And when did this happen in Kravica when 60 civilians were killed?

utterances.speaker: PW-063
utterances.text: January 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. And when were these other 30 persons killed in Bjelovac again?

utterances.speaker: PW-063
utterances.text: That was in 1992, before the 109.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: What about Fakovici, those 25? Are you referring to all the -- to all the casualties in the village of Ratkovici or are you just referring to the hamlet of Fakovici?

utterances.speaker: PW-063
utterances.text: Only Fakovici.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you tell us when this happened?

utterances.speaker: PW-063
utterances.text: I think it was the beginning of 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You mentioned Kravica now and you also speak of Kravica in your statement, on page 14, lines 18 through 25 in Serbian and in English it is also page 14, lines 10 through 19 of the transcript. That is when you had this conversation with Jean-Rene Ruez an investigator. So I'm going to quote that, P868, that is the exhibit number. Thank you, Aleksandar. So that is the exhibit number. I'm going to read it out so that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, this statement is under seal. If you want to read out a portion of that, we have to go into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. In that case, I'm not going to read it out, I'm just going to ask the witness a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This shouldn't be broadcast.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You said --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I'm not going to ask anything that is going to reveal the witness's identity. I'm asking about what had happened. I think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You said that the village of Kravica had been destroyed and torched and you mentioned how many persons were killed and so on, I'm not going to quote your statement now. This is what my question would be: Are you referring to the attack that took place on the 6th of January, 1993? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-063
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us who carried out this attack against the village of Kravica? Which forces did that? Could you say who they belonged to? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-063
utterances.text: This was done by the Muslim forces under the command of Naser Oric from Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Was the village totally destroyed and was it never used for living until the end of the war? Was that the consequence of that?

utterances.speaker: PW-063
utterances.text: It was a catastrophe, it had been destroyed, torched.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you describe it from your point of view? What it was that happened in Kravica, without revealing your own identity? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-063
utterances.text: I don't know how much I can describe because I was not in Kravica then but I do know that the Muslim forces at day break on the 6th of January, 1993, attacked Kravica with major forces and that they did what they did, namely that they killed around 60 people, that they destroyed and burned the village down. That happened on Christmas day, the greatest holiday of the Serbs. They were probably counting on that, when people are less vigilant, when they are celebrating or trying to celebrate, the Muslims did what they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you explain to the Trial Chamber what the importance is amongst the Serbs of a patron saints day and does one do anything on that day? And we are talking about Christmas there actually, sorry, it was Christmas.

utterances.speaker: PW-063
utterances.text: I already said that Christmas is the greatest Serb holiday when people do not work, when they only celebrate Christmas. That would be it briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us whether on the territory of the municipality where you were, was it the practice of Muslims to burn every hamlet and village that they entered and to kill the population regardless of whether they were civilians or not?

utterances.speaker: PW-063
utterances.text: All Serb villages in the territory of the Bratunac municipality were destroyed and torched. All of them. It was only the town that remained whereas all the villages were destroyed except for this very small area down by the Drina where the Muslims could not -- that the Muslims could not get to because they would have to go through town in order to reach that area, but all the other Serb villages were torched and destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us where the remaining surviving population went and stayed because the villages had been burned down? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-063
utterances.text: Since the Serb villages in the territory of the municipality of Srebrenica were burned down 100 per cent, all the Serb population from Srebrenica was in Bratunac and all the Serb population from the municipality of Bratunac from the burned down villages were staying in the town of Bratunac. So the town which before the war had a population of about 7.000 must have had about 12.000 at that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Will you tell us what the population was before that? You've just referred to 12.000, can you give us more information so that we can compare?

utterances.speaker: PW-063
utterances.text: The population before the war was 7.000.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you include the Muslim and the Serb population in this pre-war figure?

utterances.speaker: PW-063
utterances.text: Yes. I forgot to say that. That was both the Muslim and the Serb population. And in town the population was half-half roughly, so perhaps there were about 3.500 Serbs in town and 3.500 Muslims who had left Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: So the number of refugees, if I can put it that way, that had arrived from the areas that were destroyed and burned down by the Muslims in the Bratunac and Srebrenica municipalities had grown to 12.000, did I understand that correctly?

utterances.speaker: PW-063
utterances.text: Approximately.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us whether that was the reason why General Mladic in respect of the persons who were helping with the evacuation from Potocari -- I mean what the Prosecutor asked you here in line 14 -- no, no, not line 14. I'm going to find it now. The Prosecutor asked you during that summary, he asked you whether Mladic asked you what you thought should be done with these Muslims and he asked other interlocutors that. Was that the reason, did he want to hear the reaction of those who were victims of the Muslims or why do you think he put that question? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-063
utterances.text: I cannot say why the general had asked that. Whether he wanted to have several opinions on that. I mean, I don't understand why he asked. Maybe that what you stated just now was the reason, but I really wouldn't want to guess what the general meant by that and why he asked that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. That's what the Prosecutor asked you, today's transcript, page 12, line 23, and then he says, Mladic asked you what you thought should be done with the Muslims, if I understood that correctly. My question on that basis is as follows: This is my question to you, did General Mladic treat the Muslim population that had come to Potocari the way you had suggested? Let me not repeat everything that you had suggested.

utterances.speaker: PW-063
utterances.text: I think that this agreement was there at the Fontana Hotel. That that was the conclusion. And that in a way the general acted the way we had suggested, namely that the Muslims should be asked what it was that they wanted and if they wished to leave, that they should be enabled to do so.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I'm going to quote what it was that you said, I'll be careful not to reveal your identity. "I knew that in 1992 they left for Tuzla. I said that we should see what it was that these people wished." Was that actually done without revealing your identity yet again?

utterances.speaker: PW-063
utterances.text: Well, knowing that in 1992 when they were leaving the area of Bratunac they mostly went in the direction of Tuzla and in the direction of Kladanj our suggestion was, the suggestion of the few of us who were there around the general, was as it was for that reason, that if the Muslims wanted that, that they should be enabled to do so, if that is their wish. We did not know then what the course would be.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Before we move on to the discussion of the evacuation and the wishes of the Muslims, what they did wish and what they did not wish, let us try to get an answer to the following question: On page 20 of today's transcript, line 16 and 21 -- page 21 and one onwards, you said Rajko Dukic took care of this, and you meant the buses for Bratunac. This is what my question would be: Did I understand you correctly when you were providing an answer to the Prosecutor a few moments ago because that was the question that he had put to you?

utterances.speaker: PW-063
utterances.text: Yes, that was his answer to my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. My question for you is, should all the refugees from Potocari then go to Milici if the buses were in Milici? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-063
utterances.text: I really don't understand this question, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: It was said here that had he put the buses there. Was it logical for the buses to come to the closest possible location, to the location where those who had requested evacuation were? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-063
utterances.text: I don't see why these buses were supposed to come to Bratunac, because there was no such agreement. The agreement was that buses should leave from Potocari, pass through Bratunac, and go in the direction of Tuzla or the direction of Kladanj without staying in Bratunac at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. So you meant the buses after they left Potocari?

utterances.speaker: PW-063
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-063
utterances.text: At that moment it wasn't clear to us where these buses had come from and why they were in Bratunac, why they entered Bratunac and why they were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Does the road from Potocari lead through Bratunac or could they have taken a different road, a direct one or in a round-about way? Thank you. I mean to the territory that was under the control of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: PW-063
utterances.text: There was another road too that was up there via Jadar and Milici, but I think that that road is worse and I think that it wasn't safe at the time anyway. That is why the road via Bratunac was taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it logical then that vehicles went via Bratunac and Rajko Dukic could not have influenced that because I'm not that familiar with your relations, I have no reason to defend anyone, you included, you just said what he had said?

utterances.speaker: PW-063
utterances.text: I think that these buses were not from the Potocari actually. I think that these buses had come from the direction of Milici. They had to turn here towards Bratunac and then pass through Kravica or, rather, go towards Srebrenica, I mean Bratunac and Srebrenica from Milici. They did not take the road towards Tuzla and Kladanj at all, rather they went in the opposite way towards Bratunac and Srebrenica because these buses were not from Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I know that, but I'm asking you, was it not logical for them to get as close as possible to the people who were being evacuated, and they could not pass from Milici via Zeleni Jadar and so on because it was uncertain as to where the Muslim forces were there and there were minefields there as well and the Muslims most probably did not want to go back. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-063
utterances.text: You are not right, General. From Milici they could take a different route Tuzla and Kladanj via Vlasenica and via Zvornik. They didn't have to come to Bratunac at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. But just awhile ago you said that it was much better to go from Potocari to Bratunac the way they did rather than taking the route which was not safe via Milici. Did you say that?

utterances.speaker: PW-063
utterances.text: Yes, I did say that. Conditionally, if they went from Srebrenica via Jadar, but their buses had come from Milici. They had not been in Jadar. They took the road in the direction of Zvornik and Konjevic Polje they took a turn towards Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. We will not waste time on that. I don't understand it, let alone the Trial Chamber. In any case there was no safer road, we are talking been an area struck by war activities and there was just one road that could have been controlled by the army and the police, was that the reason why they took that road?

utterances.speaker: PW-063
utterances.text: I don't think that there was any reason whatsoever for those buses to turn up in Bratunac, from Milici to Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Was it logical for the buses to go through the territory of your municipality and for the evacuation of the civilian population to take place via the territory of your municipality, although you had attended this meeting regarding the evacuation?

utterances.speaker: PW-063
utterances.text: Yes, from Potocari. Potocari and Bratunac, they are 5 kilometres apart. And in Bratunac they could turn and they could go towards Kravica and Konjevic Polje, and there they would join the highway leading from Zvornik to Vlasenica, to the left Vlasenica and Kladanj, to the right Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. We are not going to go into speculation, we are not going to say what would have happened if other things had happened. I'm just going to talk about the security situation and who could guarantee their safety. Were you abreast of the talks that had taken place at the first and the second meeting before you attended the meeting that was depicted in the two photos, the meeting that involve the representatives of Muslims from Srebrenica? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-063
utterances.text: I attended just one meeting at 10.00. And I realised at that meeting that there had been a previous meeting and I was not aware of that meeting. I was not familiar with what had been said at that meeting. I realised that at the meeting that I attended, and I also realised that the Muslims, the delegation were supposed to state at that meeting what they wanted, or rather, only Mandzic, the president of the municipality attended the first meeting; whereas, the second meeting was attended by a larger delegation involving Camila and Nuhanovic, and then I realised that there had been a previous meeting and that that second meeting they are supposed to say what the decision was, or, rather, what the decision was that was taken up there in Srebrenica. Was I clear, General?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. You were clear. On page 37, line 7, you said that Mandzic attended the meeting alone and you said that he was the president of the municipality. Was he the president of the municipality at the time or did he introduce himself to you as a representative of the municipality or some such thing?

utterances.speaker: PW-063
utterances.text: Well, I thought that he was the president of the municipality. That's what I understood. Not that that's -- that that's what I understood, he was the president of the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. And was he the main negotiator on behalf of the Muslim delegation in his capacity as the president of the municipality?

utterances.speaker: PW-063
utterances.text: At the meeting itself I believe that Camila spoke much more than he did. He was outspoken by her. Now, in terms of hierarchy, he was in a higher position, but I would say that all three of them spoke, but Camila was the loudest. She said the most.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us now since you have just said what you did, can you then tell us whether the meeting started by General Mladic or General Karremans briefed you about the previous meeting or was the outset more spontaneous, did they start right into the heart of the matter because that's what had been agreed?

utterances.speaker: PW-063
utterances.text: Nobody briefed us about the previous meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, I think we must have our first break now, but before we break, I would like to, for the record, to note the following: On page 25 of today's transcript, line 21, you said, and I quote: "I'm restricted in the scope of questions I can put to you with regard to your position and duties." I just want to let you know this is not true. You are not restricted at all, but some questions should be put in private session if they are -- could reveal the identity of the witness. Others in open session, but you are not restricted at all. I just wanted to clarify that. We adjourn now and resume quarter past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, just a small correction for the transcript. On page 29, line 1, it says P86 and it should be P868.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. You are perfectly right. Thank you. Mr. Tolimir, please carry on your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Sir, we left it off with me asking you whether General Mladic or somebody else debriefed you about the previous meeting, or, rather, the two previous meetings and what they discussed with Mandzic and you said no. Let's continue talking about that third meeting. How did the meeting start? Who were the speakers? What did they say? How did people behave? What were your impressions?

utterances.speaker: PW-063
utterances.text: General Mladic was the first speaker. He called the meeting to order and he was the one chairing the meeting. He spoke -- well, you know, it was a long time ago. Can you give me some pointers perhaps?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me just jog your memory. In the statement that you provided, the first statement that you provided, which is P867, P867, P867, my legal assistant is -- does not hear me. P867. But I don't want the Court to produce it, I'm just going to remind you with a few words which will not disclose your identity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This is the public redacted version so that there's no problem with using this.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Thank you. Can we look at P868, pages 4 to 17.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And let me jog the witness's memory by quoting from lines 7, 8, 9, 10 and 11 and then he can go on talking and describing things in his own words. This what you stated and I quote you: "The central issue was the --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Stop, stop, stop. You said pages 4 to 17, what does that mean? Which page do you want to have displayed on the screen?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 4, the mark is 4 to 17 and I read the whole number. Can we please see page 4. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Just for the record, this is a document under seal. It will not be broadcast outside the courtroom. Please carry on, Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: To remind you, you said: "The central and the main subject of the meeting was discussions with the Muslims about their wishes. General Mladic was presiding over the meeting and the Dutch commander too, and General Mladic asked those Muslims what they wished -- whether they wished to stay in the area and if so, where they wanted to go. He suggested that if they wished to remain in the area, he would guarantee full freedom for them." That was line 12. Does this refresh your memory about the beginning of the meeting which followed immediately the events in question? I wanted to ask you this specifically: Did the general ask the Muslims what they wanted or did someone else ask them that question at the beginning of the meeting and didn't they state at the beginning of the meeting what they wanted?

utterances.speaker: PW-063
utterances.text: It was only then that I realised that there had been another meeting prior to this one. I don't know when it was held, whether it was in the morning of that day or the evening before. I couldn't conclude that. In any case, I concluded that there had been a meeting at which it was told -- Nesib was told to see what the Muslims there wanted, and when the delegation comprising the three of them arrived, they had to say what the answer received by the Muslims was. That's why General Mladic asked them whether they wanted to stay or to go. If they wanted to stay, the general would guarantee them full freedom of movement and those who were found to have participated in certain crimes, that those people would eventually be prosecuted. I see that this is the transcript of my interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Yes. You spoke to Mr. Jean-Rene Ruez. You mentioned that at the meeting the only issue was what the Muslims wanted. Can you tell the Chamber who expressed the wishes of the Muslim side at the meeting? What was that person's name?

utterances.speaker: PW-063
utterances.text: Out of the three? All three stated they wished to leave. They said only let us go. That was the wish of the people who came from Srebrenica to Potocari. Their sole wish was to leave the area. On several occasions, the general repeated that there was no need for them to leave, that they wouldn't be forced to, and that if they so wished, they were free to stay, to enjoy all freedom enjoyed by other residents of the municipalities of Bratunac and Srebrenica. However, they were quite decisive in saying that they only wanted to leave and nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did I understand you correctly that you said that no Muslims -- well, let me put it this way, did any of the Muslims present ask the general whether anyone was allowed to stay, in particular?

utterances.speaker: PW-063
utterances.text: No. Even Camila Purkovic asked the general, because she had two daughters, to assist them in leaving in the first part of the transport, whereas she wished to stay until the end. It's not in the transcript, I believe, but he said that if she wished so, he was willing to provide accommodation for his [as interpreted] daughters in the hotel and that they could leave together with her later on, but she thanked him for it and she said that she wanted her daughters to leave first. This was just a small digression which I omitted to mention previously.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Now that you mention it, was it made possible for her daughters to leave as she had requested?

utterances.speaker: PW-063
utterances.text: I think so. I have no information about what they did. That delegation did not await us in Potocari as had been agreed. It was agreed that they would wait for us in Potocari, but we'll probably get to that when we discuss the humanitarian issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Now that you mention it, it doesn't matter when I'll get to that, but you can freely tell us what the arrangement was?

utterances.speaker: PW-063
utterances.text: When we realised that the Muslims wished to leave the area, general said the new [as interpreted] from the municipality should strive to provide for the population in terms of their humanitarian needs. We understood it to be our only task at the time which we attempted to pursue as best we could. They were supposed to wait -- the delegation to wait for us there to engage in these humanitarian issues with us together so that they would be there to distribute the aid provided to the population.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-063
utterances.text: However, they did not meet us there, that is why I don't know whether Camila's daughters had left. In any case they are safe and sound and I'm sure they left the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Do you have any knowledge of the whereabouts of the Muslim delegation that was supposed to wait for you in Potocari at the moment you arrived with the humanitarian aid such as food and drinks?

utterances.speaker: PW-063
utterances.text: When we arrived in Potocari, they were nowhere to be found. We had no information of their whereabouts. After awhile, I learned where they were, but they did not wait for us then. The humanitarian aid that we brought with us had to be distributed by ourselves and it wasn't organised well. There was no order or plan. There was a large crowd, people wanted to get water and bread as well as juice and whatever we had for them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Before I ask you who distributed it, can you tell us who urgently required that the humanitarian situation be resolved, was that initiated by the Muslims or by UNPROFOR representatives or the representatives of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: PW-063
utterances.text: The general demanded it personally. He said you from the municipality should work on that. To the extent of your ability, assist the population up there with food, water, medication. It was an extremely hot day and large crowds of people, I believe there were some 20.000 of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: For the record, can you tell us whether you understood it to be your task when you say in the statement "I received the task of"?

utterances.speaker: PW-063
utterances.text: Yes, we understood it as such and that's how we implemented it, even the Municipal Assembly speaker Mr. Simic contacted the UNHCR which later also took part in providing assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 5 of this document, and you are free to refresh your memory, in lines 6 and 7 you say, I'll read it out for your sake, you say: "We sent it there to Potocari in addition to some juice and water and that lasted as long as the transportation means, the vehicles arrived." My question is this: Under whose military control was Potocari at that point in time? Who had control of the situation in Potocari?

utterances.speaker: PW-063
utterances.text: In Potocari there were the soldiers of the DutchBat as well as the VRS and the police. There were all sorts of armies around there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Were all those present tasked with providing humanitarian assistance and to aid the evacuation in keeping with the arrangement that had been reached with the Muslims, or were they there for a different reason?

utterances.speaker: PW-063
utterances.text: No, the humanitarian part was only tackled by myself and President Simic as well as those who brought the supplies. There was a water tank truck, there was a driver and a co-driver, and they distributed the water. There was a bakery lorry with bread, also with two people who distributed bread. The same goes for juice. The three from Srebrenica, however, did not make good on their promise because they were supposed to assist in the distribution of the humanitarian aid, therefore, that distribution process went on in a rather chaotic way.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-063
utterances.text: As for the soldiers, they were there as well as UNPROFOR soldiers. I believe they all had weapons and uniforms in DutchBat and they created a buffer area, a corridor between the mass of people and the road. They were trying to prevent the people from getting on to the road. They spread along the road to keep the people back.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Does that mean that there was no contact between those who arrived there and the civilian population controlled by UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: PW-063
utterances.text: The soldiers of UNPROFOR created that zone and along the road there were soldiers of the VRS as well as the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did any of those present exhibit or display aggressive behaviour towards the Muslims or did they mistreat them that you knew of?

utterances.speaker: PW-063
utterances.text: I didn't see anything of that kind. I don't think there was anything like that. I did notice that there was a lot of chaos but no one was mistreating the population.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Were there any journalists present? Were they taping the whole thing? Were they granted access? And did the VRS try to hide anything concerning the situation in the UNPROFOR base in Potocari?

utterances.speaker: PW-063
utterances.text: Well, there were people with cameras crossing the road. I don't know station they belonged to, but there were people taping the whole thing. I did see people with cameras.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: For the record, can you also answer the last part of my question, were there any attempts to cover things up, to hide anything from the public about the arrival of the Muslim population in the Potocari base?

utterances.speaker: PW-063
utterances.text: There were no attempts to hide anything and I don't think anyone could have. Nothing was hidden. Everything was public and whoever wanted to get there to watch could. It was a large area and there were journalists about.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that they did not wait for you there and that they had not organised the distribution of humanitarian aid. How did you manage the situation then? How did you distribute it? Did you improvise it on the spot?

utterances.speaker: PW-063
utterances.text: Well, there was no order to it. We just wanted to give it away because there were crowds of people who were thirsty and hungry. There was no order.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did you satisfy all those hungry and thirsty people in Potocari? Did anyone come back to you later saying they were thirsty or hungry? How did you provide that food?

utterances.speaker: PW-063
utterances.text: No, we didn't even come close to satisfying everyone. Our ability was limited and small. As I said, I believe there may have been up to 20.000 people there. With the best of our intentions even if we had that much aid it would have been difficult to make everyone happy. It was an enormous effort on our part which amounted to very little for them, I am afraid. The capacity of our bakery was 3.000 loaves of bread per day so it must have been less than a quarter of a loaf of bread per person and of course it wasn't distributed evenly. People were simply reaching out, taking all they could. It all had to be done very quickly. There was no time to make lists and distribute things orderly.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, your microphone is off.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: In your statement, you said that you invested a lot of effort, that you used your ability to the fullest even getting food and drink from Serbia?

utterances.speaker: PW-063
utterances.text: Yes, we invested a lot of effort, but for them, I believe, it was far too little. It wasn't easy for us to provide all that because we were short of those things too. Our abilities were limited and that is why we asked the people of the adjacent municipality of Ljubovija to intervene and help as well, and they did, as did those from Zvornik. But it was still only in symbolic terms. In any case, for us it was a great effort because we were short of those items as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. At page 17, which you can see on the screen, lines 14 to 20 you say as follows, and I believe you've referred to it already: "I can say one thing and that is that the job that was confined to me and to the local government was done with maximum correctness. And I think we even surpassed our material resources and capacities." And then you go on to say what you have already said about asking for assistance from Serbia. In the penultimate sentence you say: "We tried to do our best." Did I quote you correctly?

utterances.speaker: PW-063
utterances.text: Yes, you did. That is why I said that our abilities were limited. The capacity of our bakery was 3.000 loaves of bread and we also had our own population to feed. We had between 10- and 12.000 people in town who needed to be fed. Part of our production was also used for Potocari then, but we were very limited in our ability to satisfy such great numbers of people. However, we did so as best we could and in a responsible way. We took it seriously.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: In addition to the things discussed so far, such as food and water, can you tell us whether you approached the whole issue selflessly within the boundaries or limits of your ability and capacity?

utterances.speaker: PW-063
utterances.text: Of course we did. We're all human and we sympathised with the misfortune of those people, with their plight.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: In trying to alleviate the situation, did you also bring in some medical personnel such as doctors and others who could assist the wounded?

utterances.speaker: PW-063
utterances.text: Yes, our medical team from the local health clinic was also present in Potocari. In the health centre, we organised an outpatient unit with some 20 beds where we could briefly accommodate those who were more seriously ill in Potocari. We also approached that aspect.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: In your statement you mentioned the request of a person to board his family on one of the buses quickly because one of them was handicapped. Can you also describe that for us?

utterances.speaker: PW-063
utterances.text: That person recognised me, his name is Hamed. Before the war he had worked in the Municipal Assembly building as a courier. He asked me if I could take on board his uncle because he was in a wheelchair. I asked him where he was and he said that he was some 40 or 50 metres away under some trees. Then some hundred metres down the road, I spotted General Mladic. I went to see where the uncle was and then I realised that there were about 30 people in wheelchairs, or actually, not wheelchairs, but wheelbarrows. They put them in wheelbarrows to move them about because they couldn't move by themselves. When I saw the general, I realised that these people should all be put together on a bus, the handicapped ones, and I wanted to inform the general of that. I said to Hamed, wait for me here, I'll be back soon. I spoke to the general and asked him if we could put them on a bus among the first people to be transported because they are handicapped and he said no problem. Then I returned to Hamed and told him bring all of them along. However, we needed someone to push the wheelbarrows so it took about 10 minutes for them to organise themselves and we took them to one of the buses. They were put on that bus and evacuated.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Do you know whether everyone was evacuated from the territory controlled by the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: PW-063
utterances.text: Do you mean the handicapped people?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: PW-063
utterances.text: Yes, definitely. I have no contrary information.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Who brought them to Potocari from their homes?

utterances.speaker: PW-063
utterances.text: I suppose their family members.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did you bring anyone in to Potocari from the area of Srebrenica? Did you gather the population in Potocari?

utterances.speaker: PW-063
utterances.text: No, they all arrived there on their own initiative, and by whatever means they could muster. Mostly on foot. The handicapped people had probably been brought in the wheelbarrows.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did any members of the VRS in the territory of your municipality go to the area controlled by the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina in order to gather the population eventually down in Potocari?

utterances.speaker: PW-063
utterances.text: No, no one did that. They came there of their own accord.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know if any of the inhabitants from the territory of Srebrenica municipality which was under the control of the BiH Army in contacts with either you or your personnel from the municipality or at any of the meetings had expressed a desire to stay in Srebrenica, that they didn't want to join the others and go to either Kladanj or to the territory under the control of Muslims? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-063
utterances.text: Nobody asked that from me. I never heard of any case of anybody who had expressed a desire to stay in the area, either in Srebrenica or in Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did any of the Muslim representatives, the three that attended the meeting with you, demanded that any of the Muslims should stay or perhaps that they should stay, that they didn't want to leave Srebrenica since you said it yourself that Mr. Mandzic promised the freedom of movement?

utterances.speaker: PW-063
utterances.text: Well, I mentioned the case of Milo Savovic, this Lajdic [phoen] and Camila, she only was interested in her young daughters to leave on the first bus and she was prepared to leave on the last bus. Although the general offered her and her daughters to be accommodated in the hotel, to stay there until they could be evacuated. She turned that proposal down and the only thing that she asked for was what I mentioned, and that's all that she wanted.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Since we are talking about the meeting at her request, can you tell me whether General Mladic put pressure on any of them, either verbally or in any other way? Did they -- insisted on them stating a wish contrary to what they actually wanted?

utterances.speaker: PW-063
utterances.text: I even had the impression that the general suggested that they should all stay. On several occasions he suggested that, he offered them the full freedom of movement, just like to all the other population of the Bratunac and Srebrenica municipalities, on condition that people's whose hands were bloodied should be prosecuted and that militarily able-bodied men should surrender their weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you people from Bratunac, and I don't mean you personally, but you from the authorities, did you know how much weapons were there -- was there in Srebrenica, because the general insisted on them surrendering their weapons?

utterances.speaker: PW-063
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you, there were different estimates. Nobody could say with any certainty how many people were armed and how much weaponry they had, but we are certainly talking thousands. I don't know. I'm sure that we are talking about 5- or 6.000 in total. I'm talking about able-bodied men who carried arms.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 7 of your statement in lines -- or rather in line 9, you stated that you had spoken with some people and asked them where men were, and as you say in line 9, they tried to hide it from you and they said inevitably they were somewhere around, and finally turned out that they had gone into the forest, that they took to the forest to join the army. Can you tell us, and I'm talking about lines 9, 10, and 11, you have just been able to see them. Can you tell us something more about that situation, why did they hide the fact where the men were, the men that you have just mentioned, the men who were armed, some 5- to 6.000 of them in total?

utterances.speaker: PW-063
utterances.text: Well, I realised that there was something missing, people that I saw were either very young or old, and there was a gap. I didn't see any of the people that I was supposed to know, that I knew. And then I approached a person, I believe, that I inquired about Sinanovic and some others. I inquired about their whereabouts and they sounded confused and the answer was inevitably, well, here they are somewhere around here, hanging around, and then I realised that they were hiding somewhere because I simply realised that people were missing, the younger men were missing. And it turned out only later that those people had took to the woods and that they went in the direction of Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us whether those people had left fighting or without any fighting, that they had to struggle to get to the area under the control of the BiH Army? Did they leave peacefully, openly?

utterances.speaker: PW-063
utterances.text: The area of Srebrenica is very large, mostly covered with a forest, and they walked through the woods, not along any of the roads. They were armed and they fought to break through to Tuzla. They didn't take any of the roads to get there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Just for the transcripts, tell us, please, whether they took secret roads to prevent anybody from stopping them?

utterances.speaker: PW-063
utterances.text: Yes, yes. They travelled through the forest. They shied away from roads and they mostly stuck to the woods, to the well-hidden areas. They didn't go along any of the roads.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you later hear from others from the representatives of the other municipalities through whose territories they passed, or did you hear from the media whether there was any fighting, was there any invadement [as interpreted] whether the [indiscernible] information that travelled through the woods?

utterances.speaker: PW-063
utterances.text: When they got in the contact with the Army of Republika Srpska, there was fighting, of course, but they mostly chose hidden trails, and I believe that there was a lot more infighting than engagement with the Army of Republika Srpska. And when I say that there was more infighting than anything else, what I'm saying is that they themselves were not united, there were different streams. Some of them advocated surrender, they wanted to go back and surrender. The others wanted to try and break through, so there were conflicts among them. There were different situations. There were killings, there were suicides. I learned all that only later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Judge Mindua has a question for the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, while we're on the same topic put by Mr. Tolimir, while we're on the same topic of the question put by Mr. Tolimir, please correct me if I'm wrong, if I understand correctly, you were trying to distribute food, water, so you were in charge of the humanitarian needs of the population that was in your municipality. You were therefore in town. However, on page 52, line 15 of today's transcript, you say that in Srebrenica, in the greater area of Srebrenica, that area was covered by a forest. There's a great deal of forest there, and that you said that the people who you noticed were missing were most likely in the forest. They were armed and they were fighting as they were trying to reach Tuzla. My question is the following: You were in town and you were distributing humanitarian help or aid. How do you know then what was happening within the forest if indeed there were armed people and they were fighting? Is this something that you had seen or is this something that you heard of later on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me tell you, Potocari itself is located between Bratunac and Srebrenica at an accurate distance. Potocari is 5 kilometres from Srebrenica as well as from Bratunac. Srebrenica is a town in a mountainous area, in a hilly area, and the 5 kilometre road leading to Potocari goes towards Bratunac and that's where it enters a low-lying area. The refugees were in Potocari in the low-lying area, not in the hilly area. They had already descended into the low-lying area. Those that had taken to the woods, they went there from Srebrenica from the forested area, and they went in the direction of Tuzla. They had never descended into Potocari before that. Those militarily able-bodied men had immediately took to the woods from Srebrenica and why they did that, I suppose they were afraid because they -- their hands were covered in the Serbian blood and they were afraid to surrender to the Serbian army because they would have been prosecuted. And that's exactly what the general had stated at the meeting. I believe that it was their own decision to start working through the forest in the direction of Tuzla. I don't know if my answer was clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. You indeed answered to many elements of my question, but there is one aspect that's missing. You had also said that those people were armed and that they were fighting, so from where you were located, was it possible for you to realise, to notice that the missing population which you noticed was armed and was actually fighting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I heard that from my acquaintances or even friends and comrades from the Army of Republika Srpska who served in the army. I also heard that from Resid Sinanovic who had surrendered and was detained in the command of the Bratunac Brigade. He was the one who told me how it was when they tried to break through to -- through the forest from Srebrenica. Resid Sinanovic is a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much indeed. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: In order to make things clear and show that you are not saying anything that is not a fact, could you please tell us here, primarily to the Trial Chamber, what is it that you learned from Resid Sinanovic, who was either an officer or a soldier of the BiH Army? He didn't want to flee, he surrendered, he didn't want to join the break-through? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-063
utterances.text: When I visited Resid Sinanovic at the command of the Bratunac Brigade, he told me that he had set out with a group with an intention to break through to Tuzla. Together with him was his brother Muriz and his relative Medo Suljagic. The group was rather large, I can't give you any numbers. He actually didn't tell me how many there were, but the group was large and there was a conflict among them. Some of them were in favour of surrendering and the other group wanted to continue to break through. Resid Sinanovic himself wanted them to surrender, and that group chose him to lead them, or rather, to go down to the road to surrender and to negotiate with the Army of Republika Srpska about the rest of the group who had opted for surrender. And he literally told me that at that moment were chased away by your artillery, a shell fell amongst us, and from that moment on, I didn't know what had happened to my brother or to my relative or to any of the others. I started walking towards the road and the road was the one leading from Bratunac to Konjevic Polje and further on to Vlasenica. When he reached Sandici, he came to the road and that's when he came by a policeman whose name is Mirko Peric and he surrendered to him. And that police officer escorted him to the command of the Bratunac Brigade. So when I visited him we spent about an hour talking. We had been associates from 1981 to 1984. He was my chief and I was his deputy and besides our business co-operation, we were also good friends. We visited each other. We socialised. He didn't survive. I'm sincerely sorry about that. I tried, and I don't know whether you would be interested in hearing that, I tried to help him in 1992 at the very beginning of the war. I remember the date very well. It was on the 5th of May. On the 6th of May was my patron saint's day, St. George's day. He called me by phone and he told me, shall I come to your place or are you coming to my place? I need to talk to you. I need to see you. To be honest with you, the problems had already started around the town. And he lived in an apartment block whereas I lived in a family house, I thought maybe it would be easier to me to go to his building because it would be less conspicuous. Nobody would see me talking to a Muslim. I'm being honest here. Whereas that would have been a bit more conspicuous if he had come to my place. I came to his place and there he was with his wife and his two sons. Fortunately enough they are alive. They are good lads. They reside in America. They are healthy. And he says, there's something I would like to ask you. Can you talk to Deronjic and ask him to issue a pass to me. I want to visit my brother in Skopje. He had a brother in Skopje who was an active officer of the JNA, Captain Morris Sinanovic. And he says, I see that things are not good in Bratunac so I want to go down there to Skopje until things calm down. At the time Miroslav Deronjic and the SDS issued those famous passes to people who wanted to leave Bratunac. I said okay, I think I can do it. I'll go and see if I can find Deronjic and I'll let you know. Deronjic is my neighbour, or was my neighbour, and that was around 1700 hours. I didn't find Deronjic at home. His father told that he wasn't at home, and he said that he was somewhere around town. I went looking for him and sometime around 8.00 somebody told me that he was in the municipality building attending a Crisis Staff meeting. I was not working at the municipality then. How should I put this, I was not involved in political structures then because I was not a member of the SDS. I was a member of the SDP. So we did not see eye to eye politically. I went to the municipality and there there was a courier who was sitting in that first office and I asked whether Deronjic was there, and he said yes, he's in a meetings, and I said call him, I need to see him. And he said, I don't dare go tell him to come out because he said that no one should disturb him. And I said you go and tell him that I'm looking for him. Deronjic did come out after he called him, and I said to him in the hall, Deronjic, what you would do for me, do for this man, and he said what is necessary, and I said give him a pass so that he can go to Skopje. He said can it be done tomorrow? I mean, I said yes because it was already 8.00 in the evening. And he said all right, I'll give him one tomorrow morning. I went back to Resid's home and I said, Resid, you will get one in the morning. The morning of St. George's day broke out. I said it was my patron saint's day and Deronjic's house is close to mine, and I asked where Miroslav was and they said he is asleep. And I said I would need him, and they said he came only at 5.00 this morning. All right. An hour later he was still asleep. And the meantime Resid phoned me and said what's going on, and I said I'll go there now. And I went there and I woke Deronjic up, and he said let's go to the municipality and then he gave me four blank passes. I took the passes, that was 11.00 already. I went to Resid's home and we filled them out together for the four of them. Every one of them got an individual pass. And he said well, let's say good-bye now. He hails from Bjelovac which is a village 5 kilometres away from Bratunac. And he said since Skopje is far away, perhaps it's a bit late for me to leave. He also had a car that was nothing to write home about. It was a small Fiat. So then he said I'll leave tomorrow. He went home to spend the night there. I think that was his mistake. The next day his mother-in-law came to see me, she came to my home and said Resid and Beba, his wife, were returned by the police from Ljubovija. Well, how was that possible since they had passes, that's what I said, because I made sure that Deronjic gave them passes. And she said yes, but they went to Srebrenica. On the 12th Resid was taken prisoner at the command. Now, he said what had happened, he crossed the bridge on the Drina between Bratunac and Ljubovija, and from there Ljubovija is 3 kilometres into Serbia. When he was in Ljubovija, he was stopped by a patrol of the Ljubovija police and they returned him to Bratunac, to his misfortune. Then he returned and went to Bjelovac and from Bjelovac through the forest he went with his wife and children to Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I don't want to interrupt you because I thought that you felt the need to tell us all of that. Tell us one thing, do you know how Resid was killed and where he was killed? Because here you said unfortunately he had not survived.

utterances.speaker: PW-063
utterances.text: I don't know where he ended up. I just know that he is not among the living anymore. Where his life ended, I don't know. At this burial in Potocari now on the 11th of July, his remains were found by way of a DNA analysis and he was buried in July of this year.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I put an additional question to the witness, please. You told us quite a long story where he went with his wife, you mentioned different locations. How did you learn about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I learned about that from him personally. On the 12th of July when I visited him while he was detained at the command of the Bratunac Brigade. Or rather, on the 13th, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He personally told me all of this. Have I made things clearer to you now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you, indeed. Judge Mindua has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In fact, I wanted to put a question but I think that Mr. Tolimir may have asked a same question already. But just to be absolutely clear on this, witness, Mr. Resid Sinanovic you said unfortunately he did not survive, so are you confirming that you don't know under which circumstances he died?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. I just know that from the command where he had been detained and where I had visited him on that day, he was transferred to the school in Bratunac, the Vuk Karadzic school. What happened to him after that, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But you do remember the date, you remember the date of his transfer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the 13th of July. On that day when he surrendered. On that same day he was transferred to the school. Now, was it the 12th?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of which year?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1995. 1995. I mean, I'm not sure now whether it's the 12th or the 13th of July, but the year is 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Please, you started talking about Resid when you said that he had been delegated by part of the Muslims to negotiate their surrender. Did he ever carry this through, because you had described that he was hit by an artillery shell and later on he was walking on his own, choosing his own route, or did something else happen? Can you give me an answer to that?

utterances.speaker: PW-063
utterances.text: That is literally what he said to me. When the shell fell, they all started running away and then he went down the road to surrender. Perhaps it was 300 or 400 metres away from the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you just clarify something else. You said that there were conflicts among them, the Muslims. Did he mean verbal conflicts, physical conflicts, armed conflicts, what did he tell you?

utterances.speaker: PW-063
utterances.text: Verbal conflicts, unpleasant ones. He did not tell me about details, whether there was anything physical involved too. At any rate, was it a quarrel or whatever, I don't know, but there were clashes. He said that one stream was in a favour of a break-through, another stream was in favour of surrender.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. When he said that one stream was in favour of a break-through, did he say anything else about a break-through, because Judge Mindua also asked you about the number of people who were in favour of the break-through?

utterances.speaker: PW-063
utterances.text: No, he just told me a group. He did not give me any numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Later on did you find out how big that group was, that group of Muslims who wanted to break through to Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: PW-063
utterances.text: I don't think it was one group. I think it was say, tens of people, probably those thousands they did not move in one group. It was tens of groups, I'm sure. Now, I don't know how big his group was, but it's certain that there were such groups, tens of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Since certain families were trying to hide from you where it was that their men were hiding and they knew you because you were together in Srebrenica, can you tell us now whether the families, the Muslim families amongst themselves and their armed soldiers who opted for a break-through, did they know or did they agree that one group should go to Potocari and the others should try to go through the forest?

utterances.speaker: PW-063
utterances.text: Well, they knew that no one would carry out any kind of repression against women and the elderly. Of course they were afraid for themselves and they probably didn't want to surrender their weapons, and others were afraid because their hands had been bloodied, so they knew that women and children would not be harmed in any way and the elderly wouldn't either. That was probably their logic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.
