Did you know that in London in March 1992 when Lord Carrington was handing over his duty to Owen, the health ministers of the warring parties in Bosnia-Herzegovina signed a document according to which everyone one of the parties was duty-bound to give free movement to all of those who report as civilians and to pass through territory in order to get to a locality where they wanted to stay during the war? Were you aware of that since you were in government?

utterances.speaker: PW-063
utterances.text: I was not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank. Did you have an agreement with the Muslims about their evacuation? Was it on the basis of some document or agreement that they left Srebrenica and went to Tuzla? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-063
utterances.text: Deronjic did that and he had that agreement. He had a signed agreement to the effect that the evacuation had been carried out properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. What was Deronjic's role at the time because he had signed that?

utterances.speaker: PW-063
utterances.text: He was the commissioner of president Radovan Karadzic for the municipalities of Bratunac and Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you are. For the transcript, so he was the commissioner of the president of Republika Srpska yes or no?

utterances.speaker: PW-063
utterances.text: Yes, yes, he was the commissioner for the president of Republika Srpska, Radovan Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Was it not logical, then, that he would be involved in this?

utterances.speaker: PW-063
utterances.text: Absolutely. And he had that paper where there was the signature of the commander of the Dutch Battalion too, and I saw that paper that the evacuation of the civilian population had been carried out properly.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since you mentioned this, can we have in e-court P682, or rather 628 so that we'd see whether this is the document that the witness is speaking about. He said that he had seen it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise, it is P628. That is what the transcript is supposed to reflect. There was a mistake.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It was already corrected by Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can you please show page 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And we need the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I was told that we still have not a B/C/S translation, but we have two different English versions, one with the signature and the other one without. Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, earlier on this document was shown in court and I think that in the original version it is page 2 and 3. I mean, that's the Serbian version because the original version consists of an English original and an original in the Serbian language.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Now the witness can read this. There's no need for me to read it because this document has already been shown here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you read the document to yourself, witness, and can you tell us whether that's the document that you've been speaking about during your testimony? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the Trial Chamber please be in a position to follow this in English on the other side of the screen, so could the English version please be displayed for the Trial Chamber. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We will have that on the screen quite soon. We need the first page.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've read the first page.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could the witness please see page 2 of the Serbian version and can the other participants see this in English. Thank you. It's page 3, the original version in e-court. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Now the English version is missing. We have the same in B/C/S on both sides.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you produce the English version on the right side, the first page, and can the second page in Serbian remain as it is now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Now everything is on the screen according to your request.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Witness, have you read this?

utterances.speaker: PW-063
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Is that a document that you saw?

utterances.speaker: PW-063
utterances.text: Yes, I believe so. This document speaks about the evacuation which had been completed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Would you say that everything that is stated here, everything that was done was exactly what had been promised to the civilian population, the Muslim civilian population?

utterances.speaker: PW-063
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Was this document also signed by Mr. Nesib Mandzic as the representative of the civilian authorities in the Srebrenica enclave?

utterances.speaker: PW-063
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Is that what the description under his signature says, that he is the representative of the civilian authorities?

utterances.speaker: PW-063
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you ever understand his position to be anything else but the representative of the civilian authorities of the Srebrenica enclave? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-063
utterances.text: I believe that he was the president of the municipality, and here it says the representative of the civilian authorities. I don't know whether that is one in the same thing, but I believe that at the time he was the president of the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you for your testimony. Thank you for having had to repeat certain things. I would like to thank you. On behalf of the Defence, I would like to wish you a happy journey back home and God bless you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, this completes the cross-examination of this witness. I've completed the part that the Defence wanted to do in this part of the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, General. I wish you all the best and thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Tolimir. Mr. Vanderpuye, do you have re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I do, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Witness, you testified quite a lot about the information that you had concerning what was going on in Potocari with respect to the Muslim population and the involvement of the Serb authorities including VRS in that operation. Now, it is correct, though, that you were in Potocari on the 12th of July, 1995; right.

utterances.speaker: PW-063
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You were only there for a couple of hours; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PW-063
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You weren't there at all on the 13th of July, 1995; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PW-063
utterances.text: I wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: So with respect to the conduct of the VRS and other Serb authorities in relation to the Muslim population on the 13th of July, you don't have any firsthand information about what actually transpired, do you?

utterances.speaker: PW-063
utterances.text: That's correct. I wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And, sir, with respect to the representations that are made in the document that Mr. Tolimir just showed you, I don't know if we still have it on the -- in e-court? We do. It's P2628 [sic].

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: If we can go to the second page in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think I have to correct that. It is P628. You misspoke.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I did. Thank you again, Mr. President. P628.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: With respect to this document where it indicates that there were no incidents -- it says: "No incidents were provoked by any side during the evacuation, and the Serbian side observed all the regulations of the Geneva Conventions and the International Law of War ..." With respect to that representation as concerns the conduct of the VRS on the 13th, you don't have any firsthand knowledge that that's actually true, do you?

utterances.speaker: PW-063
utterances.text: I don't know what you mean when you say "firsthand." I discussed that with Deronjic and if that's firsthand then I do have information, but I wasn't there, I wasn't present.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Well, did Deronjic mention to you that he had specific information that there were killings and liquidations that were going on?

utterances.speaker: PW-063
utterances.text: No, he didn't mention that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You never discussed that with him at all?

utterances.speaker: PW-063
utterances.text: No, he never mentioned that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. You said that, and I apologise, because I don't have the exact reference in the transcript, but I believe you said in response to a question put to you by the Honourable Judge Mindua that you had -- it had struck you or you noted that in the population of Muslims gathered in Potocari, there was a component missing, and I think you mentioned that in the context of the men who took to the forest. Do you remember that part of your testimony?

utterances.speaker: PW-063
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And it struck you at the time that there were some people that were missing and so you spoke to, I assume, people in the crowd in Potocari about that, or people that you knew; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PW-063
utterances.text: I saw that middle-aged men were missing. That that part of the population was missing. I asked where they were and the answer I inevitably heard were they were somewhere around, but I didn't see them which means that they were hiding.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Well, nobody told you where they were, is that fair to say?

utterances.speaker: PW-063
utterances.text: No, no, they just said, well, they are somewhere around here in Potocari, somewhere around here.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: On the night of the 12th in Bratunac you said you had on the occasion to see a number buses with Muslim men on it, on them, do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: PW-063
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And you saw three and then you saw another set of three buses; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PW-063
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And on those buses were there Muslim men?

utterances.speaker: PW-063
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Exclusively Muslim men; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PW-063
utterances.text: Only Muslim men.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Those Muslim men that you saw on the buses would have fallen into about the age of the men that you think would have taken to the forest; is that right? That is, military aged roughly?

utterances.speaker: PW-063
utterances.text: No, I believe that even that population was older. As old as me or older than me.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: As old as you or older than you. All right.

utterances.speaker: PW-063
utterances.text: Older, well, that was 15 years ago, men between 50 and 60 years of age or even over 60 or thereabouts. It's an older part of the population but not the oldest men. 55, 60. Between 50 and 60 years of age. That would be my estimate based on what I remember. For example, there were no 30-year-old or 40-year-old men.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Now, those men, do you know where they came from? Did they come from Potocari?

utterances.speaker: PW-063
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Do you recognise any of the men on any of the buses?

utterances.speaker: PW-063
utterances.text: I recognised a man who called my name. His name was Omer Jahic. He was seated in one of the buses around the middle of the bus and he knocked on a window. I saw him, I recognised him. And he told me, or rather, invited me to get on the bus. He wanted to tell me something. The front door was open and a police officer was standing at that door. I didn't know that man. I told him there is a man in the bus who wants to ask me something, can I get on, and he says sure, go on. And so I climbed the stairs to the driver. I asked him what he wanted, and he says can you fetch me some water, and I said sure, of course. And then I said to the police officer that man asked me water, and he says well, give him if you have some. And I pointed to a 5 litre jerrycan and he was in the middle of the bus, and when I said, well, can he come closer to me, well, I asked him to send me that jerrycan, but it turns out that everybody in the bus had a jerrycan and that bus was parked right in front of the entrance to the municipality building and on the ground floor is the bathroom in the municipality building, and then we poured water into all those jerrycans, the ones that came from that bus and from the next bus behind, and I'm sure that we poured water into at least 50 jerrycans.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Did he tell you where he was from, this person that you spoke to on the bus?

utterances.speaker: PW-063
utterances.text: I knew him well. He was a native of the village of Bljeceva and before the war he was a miner in Sase in the lead and zinc mine, and he was also a deputy in the municipal council. I knew him well. He asked me, what do you think will happen to us. I asked the policeman about that and the police officer told me that they were being transferred to Batkovica and further on to Bijeljina to the collection centre down there. That's what he told me. They will be exchanged, he said. They will be exchanged for the services from Tuzla. And then I told my acquaintance don't worry, you will be exchanged, I got off the bus after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Was he staying in Srebrenica in July of 1995?

utterances.speaker: PW-063
utterances.text: I don't know, but I'm sure that he was. He was in the enclave in Srebrenica or in the territory of the municipality of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Did he tell you where he got put on that bus?

utterances.speaker: PW-063
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, while you were in Potocari on the 12th for the couple of hours that you were there, you said that you didn't see any men being separated from any of the women and children; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PW-063
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And so in your estimation based upon what you observed that night on the 12th, seeing the men on the buses, where do you suppose these men came from?

utterances.speaker: PW-063
utterances.text: That's when I saw Deronjic, on that night, and when I asked Deronjic about the buses in Bratunac and where they had come from because it -- it was not just the six buses by the municipality buildings, there were another three on one street and then there was another street behind the municipality building and there were another three there, and there were some 20 buses on the football pitch. And when I asked Deronjic about where the buses had come from, that's when he told me that that's what Rajko Dukic had planted for us, that we owed Dukic that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I understand that, but being familiar with the lay of the land were you aware that there were that many Muslim men, for example, living in Milici at the time? Or were these men from the enclave?

utterances.speaker: PW-063
utterances.text: There were no Muslims in Milici. All those were people from the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I see that it's time for the break, Mr. President, I'll have a few more questions when we return.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, it is the appropriate time. We must have the second break now and we resume quarter past 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Welcome back, witness. I'd asked you, or rather, you'd said that you didn't see any men being separated while you were in Potocari. You may know that this Trial Chamber has received evidence in this case that there were numerous hundreds of Muslim men separated from their families right there in front of the UN compound while they were being removed over the 12th and 13th of July, 1995. There's two parts to my question, first is, can you explain that? And second, did you hear about this?

utterances.speaker: PW-063
utterances.text: As for the time I spent in Potocari, it was about two hours. During that time, I did not notice any separation. Viewed from this distance and having read all sorts of things in the media, I can just say that on that a day when I was there, I didn't see that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, thank you. I don't wish to put any questions because the witness has already responded. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, in respect of the treatment of the Muslim population in Potocari, you've indicated, or at least suggested in your testimony, that you didn't see any improper treatment of that population, and of course, you may know that the Trial Chamber has also received evidence that people were in fact being shoved and kicked and being pushed on to the buses during the -- during the operation to remove them. Can you explain your observations, that's part one? And part two is, did you hear anything about that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I think that it would be better if the witness were asked a question first and to have him answer and then further questions can be asked rather than suggest to him through the question what he had heard. That would be better. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I think Mr. Tolimir may be overlooking the fact that -- are we in open session? May we go into private session for a moment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are back in open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: The question was, did you hear anything about the Muslim population in Potocari being abused in any way; that is, kicked, struck, pushed on to the buses during the operation to remove them?

utterances.speaker: PW-063
utterances.text: I really had not seen that. I was far away from the buses, perhaps 200 metres away. I just brought Nijazija to the bus and I brought the disabled people. I think that all of that was done correctly, properly. I really did not see that. This is the first time I hear that there was that kind of thing, kicking, striking people, pushing them on to buses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. Vanderpuye asked the witness about the removal of the population from Potocari and the witness testified a few moments ago that they had all asked to leave, so can he ask the witness directly whether the population was being removed or whether they were leaving on the basis of an agreement. This way the content of the witness is not being looked at, only Mr. Vanderpuye's assumptions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think the answer of the witness is quite clear. He didn't see it and he didn't -- and he heard the first time of such an allegation today. Please carry on, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Did you hear, witness, about the murder of a Muslim man who was shot by VRS soldiers against a house in Potocari before today?

utterances.speaker: PW-063
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Did you hear that there were bodies that were found by Bratunac municipal workers in the Vuk Karadzic school after the Muslim men had been held there and detained there on the 12th and 13th of July, 1995? Did you hear that before today?

utterances.speaker: PW-063
utterances.text: I did hear that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And did you hear that 40 to 50 bodies were recovered from that school?

utterances.speaker: PW-063
utterances.text: I hadn't heard of a number that big. I know that some have been found but I wouldn't be able to go into actual figures.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And did you hear that at the time or did you hear that some time after that?

utterances.speaker: PW-063
utterances.text: Later, during the course of those days. Now, was it two or five or seven or ten days later, I'd just have to guess. But during those days I did hear that there had been something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, you've read this, the text of this declaration that is dated the 17 July 1995, which talks about the evacuation being done correctly. Can you explain how that fits with your information concerning the bodies that were recovered of Muslim men from the Vuk Karadzic school in those days?

utterances.speaker: PW-063
utterances.text: I think the text of the declaration pertains to the evacuation from Potocari, and these signatures testified to that. Not the school from Bratunac because the signature of the commander of the Dutch Battalion and Nesib's indicate that it is an evacuation from Potocari, not from the school of Vuk Karadzic where a few killings had taken place. They had not had insight into that, either the commander of UNPROFOR or Mandzic. And that's what the declaration speaks of, evacuation from Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You have heard, haven't you, that a number of the men in the schools in Bratunac were brought there from Potocari, haven't you?

utterances.speaker: PW-063
utterances.text: I heard that they were brought not from Potocari but that they were gathered from the road or perhaps some had lost their way from Potocari. At first sight the school looked to me like a collection centre. People who had simply lost their way, who were wandering about. That was what I felt at first sight, and later on I had heard that there had been killings as well and -- well, I don't know about people being brought from Potocari, rather, that they were found in forests, on roads, and some at their wit's end had lost their way.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Would it have been appropriate even if this were a collection centre for those 40 or 50 people that you heard about to have been killed in those schools?

utterances.speaker: PW-063
utterances.text: How would that be appropriate? It's not appropriate to have a single person killed, how would that be appropriate? Why kill people?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I don't know whether this question is being put by the Prosecutor in order to establish the credibility of this witness of his or whether there is another basis for putting this kind of question. The man testified here about how he had openly helped the Muslims even at the time when this situation was evolving, that he went to the municipality, to the buses, et cetera, that he actually brought his own life in danger by helping others. Thank you. I think that the question is inappropriate in view of what we had heard during the testimony of this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye, what is your position?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. First, I don't think that the objection really has any basis given the question that I've put to the witness. I've asked him simply about information that he had relative to the people that he says he observed on buses and in Bratunac while he was there. That's number one. Number two is, that the nature of these acts is something I want to raise with the witness as concerns his knowledge about them, which I think is an entirely appropriate avenue to elicit information from him on. The second thing is, that if it is necessary to challenge the witness's credibility on particular issues, I think that is entirely appropriate to do so, particularly if the witness provides adverse testimony to the party that's calling him. I don't know that we've reached that per se in this circumstance, but if we get there, I'll be more than happy to let Mr. Tolimir know that's where I'm going and I will alert the Trial Chamber to that as well in accordance with the established procedure and jurisprudence, but I don't think we are there yet, and so I think that's an appropriate avenue -- appropriate way to dispose of the objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The Chamber has considered the position of both parties. We see that you were referring to the document we have still on the screen and the additional questions of Mr. Tolimir during his cross-examination. You should carry on and take into account that not only you but also Mr. Tolimir and the Chamber will have at a later stage to see and to weigh the account of this witness and his credibility. Judge Nyambe has a question for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: No, actually, I just want a clarification from Mr. Vanderpuye, that in your last submission, you are saying on certain issues you might, I don't know how to put it, declare your own witness hostile with the attendant consequences; right?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, you are right. You are right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Carry on, please, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I think I was asking you about the information you had concerning the bodies that were recovered from the Vuk Karadzic school in those days, and I asked you if you had heard about that, you indicated that you did. My next question to you was whether or not it would be appropriate, even if you thought it was a collection centre, for those killings to have occurred and you indicated that that would not be appropriate. So my question to you is, isn't that something, that is the killing of these men in the school, isn't that something that should have been brought to your attention? Now, if you need to explain your position, I think it would be appropriate to go into private session, but if you think you can otherwise answer the question without doing that, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: But perhaps before the witness answers, I think at this point in time I should make the witness aware of the Rule 90(E) of our Rules of Procedure and Evidence. Witness, I would like to read this paragraph to you. I quote: "The witness may object to making any statement which might tend to incriminate the witness. The Chamber may, however, compel the witness to answer the question. Testimony compelled in this way, shall not be used as evidence in a subsequent prosecution against the witness for any offence other than false testimony." Did you understand this provision?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, yes and no. Well, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: There's a right not to answer a question if would you incriminate yourself. This is the most important point of this rule. Mr. Vanderpuye, perhaps you'll help the witness with the question again.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: What I was asking you was, isn't the fact that Muslim men were killed in the schools in Bratunac something that should have been brought to your attention?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Maybe we should go into private session, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Where is Banja Koviljaca?

utterances.speaker: PW-063
utterances.text: Banja Koviljaca is in the Republic of Serbia. It's a town some 15 kilometres away from Zvornik, also on the banks of the Drina River. Perhaps 500 to 1.000 metres away from the Drina River, so one can easily say that it is actually on the Drina River. In Bosnia, across the river Drina is a place called Kozluk. Kozluk is across the river Drina in Bosnia, maybe that can help you get your bearings.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, that's very helpful. Did you hear about executions that took place in Kozluk?

utterances.speaker: PW-063
utterances.text: I did. As well as in many different other locations in the territory of Zvornik municipality. I read it in the press. Now, after so much time we've heard a lot of things, everything, things that we never heard before.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You mentioned that Resid Sinanovic referred to -- rather you referred to his brother Muriz and you also refer today a relative of his named Medo Suljagic. You remember?

utterances.speaker: PW-063
utterances.text: Yes, I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Medo Suljagic, can you tell us what village he is from?

utterances.speaker: PW-063
utterances.text: Medo Suljagic was from the village of Voljevica. That's about 4 kilometres away from Bratunac. He had a degree in technological science. Before the war, he had been an employee of the Kaolin factory in Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, with respect to -- sorry. With respect to Muriz Sinanovic, do you know what became of him?

utterances.speaker: PW-063
utterances.text: Muriz Sinanovic was Resid's younger brother. He was a locksmith or a machine fitter, and he also worked at the Kaolin factory. Nothing is known about their lot. When I met Resid, he told me that after the shell had fallen among them, from that moment on he didn't know what had become of his brother, Muriz, or his relative Medo, but I know that Muriz did not survive. He is nowhere to be found.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Did you hear that his remains were found in a Zeleni Jadar grave that's associated with the Kravica killings?

utterances.speaker: PW-063
utterances.text: I didn't hear that. No, I didn't hear that. I heard of Resid that he was buried last July, that the remains were found and identified and that he was buried at the graveyard in Potocari on the 11th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'm asking you, I'm sorry about Muriz --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: One moment, please. Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, just one thing. I believe that every time the person's name has been mentioned, the name has been erroneously recorded. We have Muriz and all the other different variations, just for the transcript, could we know exactly what that person's first and last names are.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Am I supposed to say that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It would be helpful.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I think it would probably be best, yes, thank you Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The person's name is Muriz, M-u-r-i-z Sinanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You see the name now on the transcript in front of you, is that written in the right way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't have that on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The court usher will help you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Muriz Sinanovic, yes, good.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Vanderpuye, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: So my question related to Muriz Sinanovic, did you hear that his remains were recovered from the Zeleni Jadar grave associated with the Kravica warehouse killings?

utterances.speaker: PW-063
utterances.text: I don't know where Muriz's remains were found. I didn't hear that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And Medo Suljagic?

utterances.speaker: PW-063
utterances.text: I didn't hear anything about Medo either.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, you said that you've heard, or rather, you said that Resid's remains were placed in Potocari; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PW-063
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And are you aware or did you hear that his remains were recovered from Cancari -- a grave on Cancari road in the Zvornik which is associated with the executions that occurred in Branjevo on the 16th of July, 1995?

utterances.speaker: PW-063
utterances.text: I've never heard of the village Cancarjevo and I don't know, I never heard about the -- Resid's remains and where they were found. On the 11th, his wife arrived and the rest of his family when the burial took place, on the 11th of July this year.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye, you should clarify that. I think that was a misunderstanding. You put to him Cancari Road and he understood it as Cancarjevo. Perhaps you should clarify that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes. What I'd asked you was if you'd heard that his remains were recovered from a grave on the Cancari Road in the Zvornik area which is a grave-site that is associated with executions that occurred at the Branjevo military farm on 16 July, 1995? Did you hear about where his remains were recovered?

utterances.speaker: PW-063
utterances.text: No, I didn't hear where they had been recovered.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You testified, I think relatively early in your cross-examination about the killings that occurred on Orthodox Christmas in Kravica in 1993. Do you remember being questioned about that by General Tolimir?

utterances.speaker: PW-063
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And you indicated, I think, that those killings occurred on the 6th of January, 1993?

utterances.speaker: PW-063
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Is that your recollection of when the Orthodox Christmas fell that year?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think we had a problem with a microphone of the interpreters. Perhaps you can put the question again.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, I think I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Is that your recollection of when the Orthodox Christmas fell that year, 1993?

utterances.speaker: PW-063
utterances.text: I remember, it's always on that date.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, given your knowledge of the circumstances surrounding that event, is it fair to say that that attack involved military combat action against VRS forces?

utterances.speaker: PW-063
utterances.text: Well, the Army of Republika Srpska may have been involved, a village may have been involved. Kravica was inhabited by the civilian population and the troops were on the lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Just bear with me for one moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Bear with me for one moment, please, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'd just like to briefly show you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye, it is two minutes before 7.00. Mr. Thayer entered the courtroom, I'm sure that he intends to update the Chamber with some problems related to the 92 bis decision. Is it perhaps appropriate to continue your re-examination tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: That would be best --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: -- before you move to another topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And I'm sure Mr. Thayer is dying to address the Trial Chamber, so I'll cede the floor to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Witness, we have to adjourn your examination for today and continue tomorrow in the afternoon 2.15 in this courtroom, but I think Mr. Thayer will address the Chamber very briefly so that there's no need now to go into private session to enable the witness to leave the courtroom. What is your estimation, Mr. Thayer?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President. It should only take me a minute or so, I think, to address the Court. Shall I -- I can switch with Mr. Vanderpuye if we have a moment, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That would be fine. Good evening and welcome, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. It's good to see you and Your Honours back again and in one piece. Here is the bottom line with respect to the 92 bis compliance: As to the witness's for whom cross-examination has been ordered, which we are treating as 92 ter witnesses in effect, all but four of those packages have been completed and sent to the Registry and, as you've probably seen, those lists are being produced and the P numbers assigned and so forth. The remaining four are -- include two very lengthy witnesses with days and days and days of testimony. It's just particularly time consuming witnesses, but we should have those completed in the very near future. So that whole category of witnesses will be completed. I understand that the Trial Chamber has particular concerns about the other category, those for whom cross-examination has not been required, and the Court naturally is curious as to why it's taking so long when, from your perspective, all you are asking for is a list of those 65 ter numbers to simply be provided. The answer is, in those 92 bis packages, there were not only documents that were introduced, tendered through those witnesses, but documents that fell into the other categories as well, documents that were shown to the witness but admitted through another witness, documents which were shown to the witness but never admitted at all. So we have the same issues with respect to those witnesses that we are dealing with. In addition to what we think is the best practice for all concerned, if at the end of the day what we want are lists that everybody, all the parties can rely on in terms of locating exhibits and knowing where they have come from and how they were used, what we would like to do and what we are now in a position to do with our resources is put those 92 bis without cross witnesses exhibits in those categories because they are spread out among those categories. The other issues, as the Trial Chamber has seen, much like with what we have already seen in the 92 bis with cross witnesses there are errors, there are errors, there are also documents which as the Trial Chamber has noted are not in the 92 bis packages. It would save a lot of time if we could do this process once as we review all these transcripts page by page to identify making sure all the correct exhibits are cited, that the exhibit lists are complete, and that we have an accurate idea of how they were used. That we apply that same methodology to this other category. I think in the end of the day it will be a much more productive project. The good news is, of the, as I count them, 55 92 bis without cross witnesses, 18 of those witnesses are victim impact witnesses who did not have any prior testimony, so that should go very quickly. Another 8 are intercept operator witnesses who I don't think will be particularly complicated, and we - I think as you've seen - we've been able to crank through I think in somewhat in excess of my original estimate of five a week, I think we've been able to crank out a few more. So I think we'll be able to come in sooner than the four months that I'd anticipated previously. I can't give the Trial Chamber a harder figure than that, but I don't think it's going to be four months, I think it's going to be closer to another 60 days. It might even be much faster than that. We'll just have to see once we sit down and start knocking out some of these other witnesses but that's where we stand now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much for this update. I realise that you said around 60 days, that means instead of four months two months if I count correctly. And this is a quite clear estimation, but referring to the first category, 92 ter, you said in the very near future, can you specify that a little bit further.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I think by the end of the week we'll be able to have at least two of those four remaining witnesses completed. I have to check with Ms. Chittenden with respect to one of them. With respect to the other, and that I don't know his PW number off the top of my head, I know it from Popovic, it's Popovic PW-168, that is an extremely extensive testimony, so that, I am afraid, I cannot help the Trial Chamber right now with the estimate. It is volumes and volumes of testimony, days and days and days of testimony. So I think alone that will probably take two weeks to organise those exhibits. That will take one person two weeks because it literally requires reading every page of the transcript and that's what this whole process has required. Ms. Stewart is advising me it's witness number 142 in this case. Thank you, Ms. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I hope you have taken into account the e-mail we have sent from the Chamber to the parties how we understand the procedure. I think there's no need to discuss it any further. Thank you for this update. I think we come back to this topic in due course. We have to adjourn now and first we have to go into private session to enable the witness to leave the courtroom. Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I would like to express my gratitude for the whole staff helping us, the court recorder, the interpreters, the technical staff, and our apologies that we are again running out of time. Thank you very much. We adjourn and resume tomorrow in the afternoon in this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 20th of October, 2010, at 2.15 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 7.10 p.m.
